newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen offering zinc, copper on high prices.
newsitem.headline: China seen offering zinc, copper on high prices.

text.p: Asian base metals premiums were being dragged down to zero or less as Chinese traders were seen offering zinc and copper on to the world market to take advantage of sky high prices, traders said on Monday.
Chinese traders were offering small parcels of copper at the London Metal Exchange cash price, leaving it to traders outside China to add their own premium, sources said.
A Hong Kong trading source said he had heard small lots of Chinese copper offered at $2,600 a tonne.
The current cash price for copper in the Shanghai area is 23,100 yuan, or $2,783, a tonne.
"I'm seeing bits and pieces of Chinese metal coming out, a few hundred tonnes, 300, 500 tonnes at a time," he said.

The same was said of zinc, with Chinese traders who bought the metal at a fixed price offering it outside China at the London Metal Exchange (LME) cash price, with no premium or at a discount, traders said.
Discounts of $10 were reported.
Traders said the zinc and copper offers aimed to take advantage of price strengths in both metals.
LME zinc eased $12 a tonne on Friday, to $1,345 a tonne. Copper touched a new one-year high of $2,548, but pulled back to $2,529, a gain of just $1 on the day.
The Chinese zinc being offered at the LME cash price or even at a discount was unregistered material that still caused raised eyebrows among North American end-users, traders said.
"If you take this stuff you cannot find a home for it," a trader in Hong Kong said, adding he had been offered Chinese special high grade ingots at a $10 discount to the LME price.
"They bought at a fixed price and as long as they see the LME price is good and they can make a profit, they are happy," he said.
A London-based analyst said a major Chinese producer had a huge short position in the market, having hedged earlier this year, and was now facing significant losses.
"There is a possibility that they are trying to talk the market down," he said, referring to reports of revved up Chinese zinc production in recent months.

One source said Zhuzhou smelter, the country's biggest producer, was considering increasing 1997 output from its current capacity of 260,000 tonnes a year to 300,000 tonnes. This could not be immediately confirmed.
Macquarie Equities brokers in London said late last week they had revised their estimate of China's 1997 zinc exports up to 400,000 tonnes, from 300,000 tonnes.
Official Chinese customs figures show January to April 1997 zinc exports were 162,145 tonnes, up a year-on-year 131.1 percent.

China's copper exports were also up significantly, customs figures showed. Unwrought copper and copper materials exports in the January to April period were 58,496 tonnes, up a year-on-year 115.6 percent.
The head of a Chinese smelting operation said these figures were mostly based on tolling, in which copper is imported duty-free for processing and re-export.
He said the Chinese government was tightly controlling exports and had not issued any licences for copper to move out.
Domestic production was being consumed domestically, he said, adding that consumption was normal to slow as cash remained tight.

Analysts said they expected to see an easing of credit in China in the second half of 1997, and this could coincide with an expected dip in LME copper prices as Europe winds down for the Northern Hemisphere summer.
-- Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-8544
